deep.reconstruction:
Five separate jottings. The previous page (Hilbert's 'characteristic function', Brill–Hurwitz) and the next page (his theorem on definite forms) suggest c. 1888–1891. That date is an inference, not established.

(1) Primes satisfying a linear equation. Problem: solve a p + b q + c = 0 with given integers a, b, c and unknown primes p, q. Question: are there infinitely many solutions? Special cases written down:
- p - q = 2 (twin primes);
- p - q = 2r with p, q, r all prime.
In the second case parity forces p and q to be odd (if q = 2, p would have to be even). Examples: 7-3 = 2*2, 11-5 = 2*3, 13-3 = 2*5. The general equation also contains binary Goldbach: take a = b = 1, c = -2N.
This is essentially the wording of the 'arithmetic' part of Hilbert's 8th Paris problem (1900): solvability in primes of a x + b y + c = 0, and the twin-prime question. The variant p - q = 2r is not in the 1900 text.

(2) A research programme. 'Treat Weierstrass's theory of elementary divisors and the Riemann–Roch theorem by my method of the terminating process (Abbruchverfahren) and of the characteristic function.' This refers to the 1890 Annalen paper 'Über die Theorie der algebraischen Formen': finite free resolutions (the syzygy chain terminates) and the Hilbert function/polynomial. No derivation is given.

(3) Prime values of polynomials. 'Prove that the sequence f(0), f(1), f(2), ... contains at least one prime.' The hypotheses are left implicit. My supplement: f is an integer polynomial, irreducible, positive leading coefficient, and the values have no fixed common divisor. This is the 'at least one prime' form of the Bunyakovsky conjecture. Applying it to f(x + k) for every k gives infinitely many primes, so the two forms are equivalent.

(4) Philosophical aside. Mathematics as
- a tool or instrument (a means only, sanctified by its end; physics, chess, arithmetic puzzles);
- a toy;
- the highest science;
- for some ideally disposed natures, mental gymnastics apparatus.

(5) Fundamental theorem of algebra; the sketch continues onto the next page.
- Put x = xi + i*eta and write f = phi + i*psi.
- Roots of f are the intersection points of the real curves phi = 0 and psi = 0. For f without multiple roots these intersections are separate (Hilbert corrected 'reell' to 'getrennt').
- Transversality (my addition): at a root, the Jacobian of (phi, psi) equals |f'(z)|^2 > 0, so each intersection is transversal.
- 'An algebraic curve can never end.' So if, under continuous change of the coefficients, the number of intersection points is to drop, two of them must coalesce.
- Next page: for real f this means either f = f1*p^2 with p a real quadratic (a double conjugate pair; two conditions) or f vanishes at a real point. Both can be avoided.
- Reason: the definite forms make up a convex, hence connected, open set, so any definite f can be joined to any other without crossing forms with a real zero. The double-pair locus has codimension 2 and can be dodged.
- Hence the number of intersection points is constant on definite forms. Comparing with a model such as a product of distinct factors x^2 + c_i would give n roots.
- This is the method Hilbert used for definite forms in 1888, combined with Gauss's 1799 picture of the curves Re f = 0 and Im f = 0.
errors: Item (1) states no hypotheses on a, b, c, and the infinitude question needs local conditions. If a, b, c are all odd and p, q are both odd, then a p + b q + c is odd and cannot be 0. Coprimality (as in the 1900 wording 'each prime to the others') is not enough: p - q + 1 = 0 has only the solution (p, q) = (2, 3). Signs also matter: p + q + 1 = 0 has no solution at all.

Item (3) gives no hypotheses on f. The claim is false without irreducibility and the no-fixed-divisor condition, e.g. f(x) = x^2 + x + 2 always gives even values greater than 2. With the hypotheses it is still unproved for degree >= 2 (Bunyakovsky).

The FTA sketch is heuristic in four places. (a) 'An algebraic curve can never end' is exactly the gap in Gauss's 1799 proof, closed rigorously only by Ostrowski (1920). (b) It is not shown that intersection points cannot escape to infinity; this holds because the leading coefficient stays nonzero, but it is unstated. (c) The statement that a codimension-2 algebraic subset does not disconnect the open cone of definite forms is used tacitly. (d) A base case with exactly n intersection points must be checked separately, and as given the argument covers only definite (even-degree, root-free) real f. The reduction of general f to this case (e.g. via f times its conjugate, or adding a large definite term) is not given on this page.
Persistence of a transversal intersection under perturbation needs the implicit function theorem (Jacobian |f'|^2 nonzero), which is not mentioned.

results.what: Question whether a p + b q + c = 0 has (infinitely many) solutions in primes p, q; special case twin primes p - q = 2
results.modern_name: Linear equations in two primes / generalized twin prime and binary Goldbach problems (part of Hilbert's 8th problem); still open
results.usually_credited_to: Twin primes: folklore, de Polignac 1849. The linear-equation formulation is known from Hilbert's 1900 Paris address, problem 8.

results.what: Infinitely many primes p, q, r with p - q = 2r
results.modern_name: Ternary linear equation in primes; solvable infinitely often by the Hardy–Littlewood–Vinogradov circle method
results.usually_credited_to: Vinogradov 1937 and van der Corput 1939 (ternary problems in primes); general ternary linear equations in primes by Hua and others

results.what: Programme: derive Weierstrass elementary divisor theory and Riemann–Roch from free resolutions (Abbruchverfahren) and the Hilbert function
results.modern_name: Homological/Hilbert-polynomial approach to Riemann–Roch and to modules over a PID (structure theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert-polynomial approach to arithmetic genus: Hilbert 1890, Severi, Lasker, later Serre/Grothendieck. Elementary divisors via module theory: E. Noether school (1920s).

results.what: Prove that f(0), f(1), f(2), ... contains a prime
FTA via intersections of Re f = 0 and Im f = 0, with continuous deformation of the coefficients inside the convex set of definite forms avoiding the codimension-2 locus f = f1*p^2
results.modern_name: Continuity/homotopy (degree-theoretic) proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra; discriminant locus of real codimension 2
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss 1799 (geometric picture), Gauss 1849; rigorous continuity proofs later (Ostrowski 1920, degree theory)

results.what: Remark classifying mathematics as tool / toy / highest science

deep.surprise_reason: The prime-number questions are an early private version (c. 1890) of what Hilbert published as part of problem 8 in 1900. That is a nice genealogical detail, but the problems were already folklore (twin primes, Goldbach, Bunyakovsky) and no new result is proved. The FTA sketch is a variant of Gauss's argument combined with Hilbert's own 1888 deformation method for definite forms. The Riemann–Roch / elementary divisors programme note is of some historical interest but contains no content.

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); z=x+I*y; f=expand(z**3-2*z+5); phi=re(f); psi=im(f); fp=expand(3*z**2-2); simplify(Matrix([[diff(phi,x),diff(phi,y)],[diff(psi,x),diff(psi,y)]]).det()-(re(fp)**2+im(fp)**2))
checkable.asserts: Jacobian of (Re f, Im f) equals |f'(z)|^2, so intersections of phi=0, psi=0 at simple roots are transversal (result 0)

checkable.sympy: all(isprime(p) and isprime(q) and isprime((p-q)//2) and (p-q)%2==0 for p,q in [(7,3),(11,5),(13,3),(17,3),(19,5)])
checkable.asserts: Examples of p - q = 2r with p, q, r prime

checkable.sympy: [(p,p+1) for p in primerange(2,10000) if isprime(p+1)]
checkable.asserts: p - q + 1 = 0 (a, b, c pairwise coprime) has only the solution (2, 3), so coprimality alone does not give infinitely many solutions
If a, b, c are odd and p, q are odd, a p + b q + c is odd, hence nonzero (result 1)
x^2 + x + 2 is always even, so f(n) can be prime only if f(n) = 2; hypotheses are needed in the f(0), f(1), ... claim

checkable.sympy: x,t=symbols('x t',real=True); g=t*(x**2+1)**2+(1-t)*(x**4+x**2+1); [minimum(g.subs(t,s),x) for s in [0,Rational(1,3),Rational(2,3),1]]
checkable.asserts: A convex combination of definite quartics stays definite (minimum > 0), illustrating connectivity of the definite cone

checkable.sympy: x,a,b,c,d=symbols('x a b c d'); discriminant(x**4+a*x**3+b*x**2+c*x+d,x)
checkable.asserts: The multiple-root locus is the hypersurface disc = 0. Within it, the f = f1*p^2 stratum (double conjugate pair) has real codimension 2, matching Hilbert's 'two conditions'.

transcription_corrections: 'der Weierstrass'schen Theorie' should read 'die Weierstrass'sche Theorie der Elementartheiler und den Riemann=Roch'schen Satz behandeln'. It is the object of 'behandeln', a separate programme note, not part of the prime problem.

In the FTA paragraph Hilbert crossed out 'n complexe Wurzeln' after 'Grades' and wrote 'eine Wurzel'. He also replaced 'reellen' by the superscript 'getrennten' (intersections 'in getrennten Punkten').
'Werkzeug' is crossed out and replaced by 'Geräth' above the line, as transcribed.
'eine Waffe, das nicht immer gut umgangen werden kann' is more likely 'eine Waffe, die nicht immer gut umgangen [= mit der umgegangen] werden kann'. The reading is uncertain.
The last parenthesis reads roughly '(Manchen ideal angelegten Naturen als geistiges Turngeräth.)', with 'auch' struck out.
'Spielzeug (bessere Dienst am Schach kann ...)' is uncertain. Possibly '(besser Dienen am Schach kann ... werden)'.
